stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Immunologists long held that immunological memory belongs only to the adaptive immune system, whose T and B cells "remember" specific pathogens. Innate cells such as macrophages were thought to respond the same way to every encounter. Yet when researchers exposed mouse macrophages to a fungal cell-wall compound and then, weeks later, to an unrelated bacterium, the cells produced much stronger inflammatory signals than unexposed macrophages did. This heightened response, lasting long after the first exposure, suggests that innate cells can keep a kind of memory of their own.
choices: To describe an experiment in which macrophages were exposed to two different substances weeks apart
To challenge the view that only the adaptive immune system is capable of immunological memory
To argue that innate immune cells remember specific pathogens as precisely as T and B cells do
To explain why T and B cells respond more strongly to pathogens they have encountered before
explanation: The text opens with what immunologists "long held": memory belongs only to the adaptive system. "Yet" brings in the macrophage experiment, and the last sentence concludes that innate cells can also keep a kind of memory. The experiment is there as evidence against the opening belief, so the text's purpose is to challenge that belief.

A.why: You described what most of the text contains instead of what it is for. The experiment is evidence; the text uses it to undercut the belief stated at the start.

C.why: You took "a kind of memory" much further than the text does. The second exposure was to an unrelated bacterium, so the text shows no pathogen-specific memory, and it never says the innate response matches T and B cells in precision.

D.why: You latched onto the background in the first sentence. The text mentions adaptive memory only as the view it is about to complicate, and it never explains how that memory works.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Textile historians have often described the arrival of the spinning wheel in medieval Europe as a sudden revolution that swept the hand spindle aside. Guild records from thirteenth-century Flanders complicate that picture. Several cloth-making towns banned wheel-spun yarn from the warp threads of fine woolens, judging it too uneven, and allowed it only in the weft. Spindles therefore stayed essential in those workshops for generations. The wheel did transform yarn production, but its adoption was partial and contested rather than swift and total.
choices: To suggest that the spinning wheel's adoption was more gradual and uneven than often portrayed
To argue that the spinning wheel had little real effect on medieval yarn production
To present the regulations that Flemish towns imposed on the yarn used in fine woolens
To explain why wheel-spun yarn was considered better suited to weft than to warp
explanation: The text starts with what historians "have often described": a sudden revolution. It then says the guild records "complicate that picture" and ends by calling the adoption "partial and contested rather than swift and total." The purpose is to correct how quickly and completely the wheel is said to have taken over, while still granting that it transformed production.

B.why: You read a warning against overstating as a full rejection. The author says outright that the wheel "did transform yarn production". What the text disputes is how fast and how fully it was adopted, not whether it mattered.

C.why: You picked what the middle of the text contains. The Flemish rules are evidence the author uses to complicate the "sudden revolution" story, not the reason the text was written.

D.why: You treated a passing detail as the main point. The text does say guilds found the yarn "too uneven," but that is only a brief reason inside the evidence, not what the passage sets out to do.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: For decades, metallurgists have relied on a dependable rule: shrinking the crystalline grains inside a metal makes it stronger, because the boundaries between grains block the defects that allow the metal to deform. Recent work suggests the rule has a floor. When a team produced copper samples with grains only a few nanometers across, the samples proved softer than ones with somewhat larger grains. At that scale, the researchers propose, the grain boundaries themselves begin to slide, opening a new route to deformation.
choices: To describe a technique for producing copper samples with grains only a few nanometers across
To explain how the boundaries between grains strengthen a metal by blocking its defects
To show that a long-relied-on rule about grain size fails to hold below a certain scale
To argue that reducing grain size generally weakens metals rather than strengthening them
explanation: The text states a rule metallurgists "have relied on" and then says it "has a floor." The nanometer-scale copper result and the sliding-boundary explanation show where the rule stops working. The purpose is to show its limit, not to describe the experiment or throw the rule out.

A.why: You chose the experiment, which takes up much of the text. The text never describes how the samples were made. It only reports what they revealed about the rule.

B.why: You picked the background that comes before the turn. The explanation of how boundaries block defects is set up so the text can then show where it stops applying.

D.why: You turned a limit into a reversal. The text says the rule "has a floor". It still holds above extremely small sizes, so smaller grains do not "generally" weaken metals.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Shell middens, the vast mounds of discarded mollusk shells found along many coastlines, have traditionally been interpreted as refuse heaps: places where generations of people dumped the remains of their meals. Excavations at a large midden on the Gulf coast, however, uncovered several thin layers of packed clay laid down at regular intervals, with hearths and postholes on each layer. Such features suggest that at least some middens were deliberately built up as raised living surfaces, not merely accumulated as waste.
choices: To question the assumption that shell middens were nothing more than piles of discarded food remains
To describe the clay layers, hearths, and postholes uncovered at a coastal midden excavation
To argue that shell middens were built as living surfaces rather than used for discarding waste
To support the view that middens formed gradually as meals were discarded over many generations
explanation: The text opens with the traditional reading of middens as refuse heaps. "However" introduces excavation evidence, and the final sentence concludes that "at least some" middens were built as living surfaces, "not merely" waste. The purpose is to question the idea that middens were only garbage.

B.why: You described the evidence instead of what it is used for. The clay layers and hearths are there to undercut the refuse-heap interpretation.

C.why: You missed the hedges. "At least some" and "not merely" mean the author still allows that middens held waste, and the claim covers only some of them. This choice makes it all middens and drops the waste role entirely.

D.why: You picked the view the text is arguing against. The refuse-heap interpretation is the traditional belief that "however" turns away from, not the one the evidence supports.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Histories of Western concert music often claim that improvisation disappeared from the classical stage early in the nineteenth century, as performers came to treat the printed score as an untouchable text. The personal papers of the Viennese pianist Henriette Vass suggest a slower decline. Her annotated programs from the 1870s show that she routinely improvised short preludes to link the pieces she performed, and reviews of her recitals mention these passages without surprise, implying that audiences still expected them.
choices: To describe the annotated programs and recital reviews preserved among Vass's personal papers
To argue that most pianists of the 1870s improvised entire works instead of playing from scores
To explain why nineteenth-century performers began to treat printed scores as untouchable texts
To challenge a common claim about when improvisation stopped being part of classical performance
explanation: The text begins with what histories "often claim": improvisation vanished early in the nineteenth century. Vass's papers "suggest a slower decline", showing that she and her audiences treated improvisation as normal in the 1870s. The purpose is to challenge the usual timeline.

A.why: You named the source material, which fills most of the text, instead of its job. The programs and reviews are evidence against the standard timeline.

B.why: You generalized one pianist into "most pianists" and short linking preludes into "entire works." The text supports neither.

C.why: You focused on a clause inside the belief the author is questioning. The text mentions the score as "untouchable" only as part of that claim, and never explains why the attitude arose.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Linguists have frequently assumed that a language's sound system changes only gradually across generations, as each cohort of children learns to speak slightly differently from its parents. A long-term study of one fishing town complicates that assumption. Recordings of the same twenty adults, made over thirty years, show that many of them shifted their vowel pronunciations substantially in middle age, moving toward a newer pattern adopted by younger speakers. Change, it seems, need not wait for a new generation.
choices: To argue that sound change is driven mainly by adults rather than by children acquiring language
To present recordings showing how residents of a fishing town pronounced vowels over three decades
To complicate the assumption that sound change happens only from one generation to the next
To show that adults' pronunciation tends to remain stable once their speech habits are formed
explanation: The text opens with what linguists "have frequently assumed" and says the study "complicates that assumption." It closes with "Change... need not wait for a new generation." The adult recordings show that change isn't limited to passing from one generation to the next, which is the narrow point the text makes.

A.why: You inflated "need not wait" into "driven mainly by adults." The text shows adults can change too. It never says they matter more than children, and the adults were moving toward a pattern younger speakers had already adopted.

B.why: You described the study, which fills most of the text, instead of asking why the author brings it up: to complicate the generational assumption.

D.why: You reversed the finding. The recordings show many adults changing their vowels "substantially in middle age," which is the opposite of stability.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Paleobotanists have long used the shape of fossil leaves to estimate ancient temperatures: in today's forests, trees with smooth-edged leaves dominate warm regions, while toothed leaves are more common in cool ones. A recent survey urges caution. Among living trees growing along rivers and lake shores, toothed leaves were common even in warm climates, apparently because they help leaves grow quickly in wet soils. Since many fossil leaves come from such waterlogged settings, estimates based on them may run too cold.
choices: To argue that fossil leaf shape provides no useful information about ancient temperatures
To describe how toothed leaves help trees grow quickly in wet soils near rivers and lakes
To suggest that ancient climates were warmer than fossil leaves from dry settings indicate
To identify a reason that a common method of estimating past temperatures may mislead
explanation: The text sets up a method paleobotanists "have long used," then "urges caution." The survey of riverside trees shows a bias: toothed leaves in warm, wet places can make fossil-based estimates "run too cold." The purpose is to point out one way the method can mislead, not to reject it.

A.why: You treated a warning as a rejection. The text "urges caution" about one bias in fossils from wet settings and never says leaf shape is useless.

B.why: You picked a detail from the evidence. The wet-soil advantage of toothed leaves is the cause of the bias the author flags, not the point of the text.

C.why: You attached the problem to the wrong setting. The text says estimates may run too cold for fossils from waterlogged settings, not dry ones.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Land managers have generally treated the removal of invasive plants as a reliable way to restore native communities: clear the invader, the reasoning goes, and the original species will reclaim the ground. A twelve-year study of riverside plots from which an invasive shrub had been cut paints a less hopeful picture. Native wildflowers returned to only a third of the cleared plots. In most of the others, the shrub's leaf litter had altered the soil's nitrogen levels, and fast-growing weedy grasses, not natives, filled the openings.
choices: To report how an invasive shrub's leaf litter changed nitrogen levels in riverside soils
To cast doubt on the idea that removing an invader reliably allows native species to return
To argue that land managers should stop removing invasive plants from riverside areas
To show that native wildflowers recover more quickly in cleared plots than weedy grasses do
explanation: The text opens with what land managers "have generally treated" as reliable. The study then "paints a less hopeful picture": natives came back to only a third of the plots. The purpose is to cast doubt on the assumption that removal alone reliably restores native plants.

A.why: You picked a mechanism from the evidence. The nitrogen change explains why natives often failed to return, but the text reports it to undercut the managers' assumption, not for its own sake.

C.why: You read a challenge to a belief as a policy recommendation. The text questions whether removal is enough by itself, and natives did return in a third of the plots. It never tells managers to stop.

D.why: You reversed the result. In most cleared plots, weedy grasses, "not natives," filled the openings.
